requirements.text: The business must maintain a register of business entities, the umbrella concept covering all customers, vendors and employees.
Each business entity must be identified by a single company-wide business entity number that is unique across every party, regardless of whether the party is a customer, a vendor or an employee.

The business entity number must be usable to link a party to information held in other areas of the business (sales, purchasing, HR), with the party register acting as the integration point for the rest of the company.
requirements.obj: party to information in other business areas

requirements.text: The business must be able to recognise that the same party may play more than one role at the same time (for example, an employee who is also a retail customer), and the system must not force a party into a single role.
Each business entity record must carry a last-changed timestamp recording when it was last updated, so the business can understand the currency of the party register.
Each business entity record must carry a globally unique record identifier that exists to support data replication between systems.
The globally unique record identifier has no business meaning, is not a business key, must be treated as technical metadata and needs no business reporting.
The business must record every person it deals with, identified by the same company-wide business entity number as the business entity, without a separate person identifier.
Every person must be a business entity, while not every business entity is a person, since organisations such as vendors and stores are also business entities.
The business must record the primary type of each person, which classifies why the person exists in the systems.
The recognised primary person types are store contact, individual (retail) customer, salesperson, employee (non-sales), vendor contact and general contact.
The business must be able to count, segment and filter people by their primary type in every analysis (for example, how many individual customers are held in Germany).
The list of person types is a small, fixed set of codes held in the person record itself rather than in a separate reference list.
The warehouse must present the meaning of each person type code in business language rather than as the two-letter code.
The business must record each person's first name, middle name or middle initial, and last name.
The business must record an optional courtesy title (for example Mr. or Ms.) for use in correspondence.
The business must record an optional surname suffix (for example Sr. or Jr.).
The business must record a name style indicating whether a person's name is presented in western order (first name then last name) or eastern order (last name then first name).
Any report or output that displays a person's full name must be able to honour the recorded name style and must not assume western ordering.
requirements.obj: name style in full name display

requirements.text: Middle name, title and suffix are optional, and reporting must cope with people who have none of them.
The business must record each person's email promotion preference, which expresses the consent given for marketing contact.
The recognised email promotion preference levels are: no email promotions, email promotions from AdventureWorks only, and email promotions from AdventureWorks and selected partners.

Marketing and campaign selection must be able to filter by email promotion preference and distinguish the company-only case from the company-and-partners case, because the two permit different uses of the person's details.

The business must be able to state what a person's email promotion consent preference was in the past, not only what it is now, and historical tracking of consent changes must be introduced by the warehouse if the business requires an audit trail.
The business must retain additional contact information held for a person in a free-form structured (XML) format.
The business must retain demographic information collected from online shoppers, such as hobbies and income, which is captured for sales analysis.
Demographic content must be made analysable (for example, segmenting customers by income band or interest) rather than stored as an opaque block.
Access to demographic and additional contact information must be treated as sensitive and restricted separately from ordinary name and contact reporting.
Each person record must carry a last-changed timestamp so the business can know how current a person's details are.
The business must be able to identify person records that have not been touched for a long time.
The business must record the email addresses of people.
A person may have more than one email address, each numbered within the person.
The business must be able to report all of a person's email addresses, not just one.
requirements.obj: all email addresses of a person

requirements.text: An email address belongs to exactly one person and is meaningless without that person.
The business must be able to identify people who have no email address at all, since they cannot be reached by email campaigns regardless of promotion preference.
Each email address must carry its own last-changed timestamp, independent of the rest of the person's record.
The warehouse must retain superseded email addresses historically so the business can understand whether an address currently on file is still the one previously used in a campaign.
The business must record the telephone numbers of people.
A person may have several telephone numbers, and each number is qualified by the kind of phone number it is.
The business must maintain a reference list of phone number types, each with a name describing the kind of number (for example home, work or mobile).
Reporting must be able to select a person's telephone number by type (for example, the work number of every store contact in Bavaria).
A telephone number belongs to exactly one person.
Each telephone number must carry its own last-changed timestamp.
Phone number type names must be named consistently over time, because a rename affects the meaning of historical reporting.
The business records a sign-in credential for a person, consisting of a protected (hashed) password value and the random value used to protect it.
The sign-in credential relates to the person's email account, indicating that people can sign in to company systems such as the online store.
Credentials must never be brought into the warehouse as readable values, reported on, or exposed to analysts.

The only business-relevant facts about a credential are whether a person has one and when it was last changed, showing whether the person has a self-service account and how recently it was maintained.
If the business does not need to know whether a person has a credential and when it was last changed, the whole credential record should be excluded from scope.
A credential record is attached to a person by the same business entity number, and one person has at most one credential.
The business must record postal addresses, each identified by its own address number.
An address consists of a first street address line, an optional second street address line, a city, a postal code, and the state or province in which it sits.
The state or province of an address determines its country, so the country is known indirectly through the state or province rather than being stated on the address itself.

The business must record the geographic location (latitude and longitude) of an address to support mapping, distance and territory analysis, such as showing reseller stores on a map or measuring how far customers are from a store.
Addresses must be reportable at each geographic level: street, city, postal code, state or province, and country or region.
Each address carries a last-changed timestamp so the business can see when address details were corrected.

An address is recorded once and can be shared by more than one party, such as several employees of the same reseller store or a household; the business must not assume an address belongs to a single party.

The business must decide whether historical address values must be retained, so that past activity can be reported against the address as it stood at the time, given that address records are edited in place and later corrections may affect analysis of where a customer was at the time of a past order.
The business must record which addresses belong to which business entity (party), and in what capacity.
A party can have several addresses, and the same address can serve several parties.
Every party-address relationship must carry an address type stating the role the address plays for that party, such as Billing, Home or Shipping.
A party may have different addresses for different purposes, for example one address to bill and another to ship to.
The combination of party, address and address type makes a party-address relationship unique.
A party may hold the same address under two different address types, such as an address that is both billing and shipping address, and both relationships must be visible.
The business must maintain a reference list of address types, each with a descriptive name.
The business must be able to answer what the shipping address of a given customer is.
The business must be able to answer which customers ship to a given city.
Each party-address relationship carries its own last-changed timestamp.

If the business needs to know which address a party used at a given point in the past, the warehouse must build and keep the history of party-address relationships, because the source holds only the currently valid set.
The business must be able to identify parties with no address on file, since they cannot be shipped to or invoiced by post.
The business must maintain a reference list of countries and regions, each identified by its ISO standard country or region code and carrying its name.
The business must maintain a reference list of states and provinces, each identified by its own number and carrying an ISO standard state or province code and a descriptive name.
Every state or province belongs to exactly one country or region.
A country or region may contain many states or provinces, and some may contain none.
A state or province carries a flag indicating that no genuine state or province code exists and that the country or region code is used in its place.
Reporting must handle the no-genuine-code flag gracefully and must not present a substituted country code as if it were a real state or province code.
Every state or province is assigned to a sales territory, linking where an address is to the part of the sales organisation responsible for it.
The business must be able to roll addresses, and therefore customers, stores and employees, up to sales territory via their state or province, to support territory-level sales and coverage reporting.
Only the assignment of a state or province to a sales territory is available in this area, so the warehouse must obtain territory descriptions from the sales area.

The business must decide whether territory assignments of states or provinces should be tracked over time, so that past performance can be reported on the territory structure that applied at the time, since reassignment otherwise changes all historical geographic roll-ups.
Country, state and territory reference lists each carry a last-changed timestamp.
Country and state or province names used in customer-facing output and reporting must be consistent and current, and renames must be visible rather than silent.
requirements.obj: country and state or province names

requirements.text: The business must record which people act as contacts for which organisations, such as the named individual who is the contact at a reseller store or at a supplier.
A contact relationship links two parties: the organisation (a business entity) and the person acting as its contact.
Every contact relationship must carry a contact type describing the role the person plays for that organisation.
The business must maintain a reference list of contact types, each with a descriptive name.
The same organisation may have several contacts in different roles, and the combination of organisation, person and role makes a contact relationship unique.
The same person may act as a contact for more than one organisation and may hold more than one role at the same organisation.
The business must be able to answer who the contact is at a given store and in what role.
requirements.obj: contact and role at an organisation

requirements.text: The business must be able to answer which organisations a given person represents.
Each contact relationship carries its own last-changed timestamp.

If the business needs to know who the contact was at a given time, such as when investigating a past order, the warehouse must retain the history of contact relationships, because the source holds only the current set.

Reporting must clearly distinguish which side of a contact relationship is the organisation and which is the individual, since both are business entities using the same party number and the distinction comes from the party's role rather than from the relationship.
requirements.obj: organisation and individual in contact relationship

requirements.text: The business needs a single view of a party that brings together, for one party number, the party's name and type, all email addresses, all telephone numbers with types, all addresses with types, and all organisations the party is a contact for.

Reporting must correctly reflect that a party's email addresses, telephone numbers, addresses and contact relationships are one-to-many, and must not assume a person has exactly one address, email or phone number.
The single view of a party must remain correct when a party plays several roles at once.
Every record in this area carries only a last-modified timestamp, and the operational system holds the current state only and overwrites previous values in place.

The business has no history today for a person's name, marketing consent, email address, telephone numbers, address street, city or postal details, the addresses a party uses and for what purpose, contact roles for organisations, or the sales territory of a state or province, all of which change and matter analytically.

The warehouse must preserve the full history of change for a person's name, marketing consent, email address, telephone numbers, address details, party-address relationships, contact relationships and territory assignment of states or provinces, so past activity can be reported against the party details that applied at the time.
The last-changed timestamp on each record is the only change signal the source provides, and its reliability must be confirmed with the operational system owners.

The source provides no deletion marker or status flag in this area, so removed parties, addresses or relationships simply disappear; the business must state whether removals need to be detected and retained.
The business needs visibility of incomplete party records: people without an email address, without a phone number, or without any address.
The business needs visibility of duplicate people, meaning the same individual registered more than once under different party numbers, because this affects customer counts and campaign accuracy.
The business needs visibility of addresses whose geographic location is missing, since they cannot be mapped or measured for territory purposes.
Reporting should highlight states or provinces carrying the no-genuine-code flag rather than hide them, as they signal incomplete geographic reference data.
requirements.obj: states or provinces with no genuine code

requirements.text: Reference lists for address type, contact type, phone number type, country or region, and state or province must be complete, so that every relationship and address resolves to a named type, country or region.
Unresolvable references to types, countries or regions, or states or provinces must be reported as data quality defects.

This area holds personal data about identifiable individuals, including names, home addresses, private email addresses, telephone numbers, geographic coordinates, marketing consent, and self-declared demographics including income.
Access to person-level detail must be restricted to roles with a legitimate business need.
Aggregated reporting, such as counts by region, by person type and by consent level, should be available more widely.
Sign-in credentials must be excluded from all analytical use.
Marketing consent must be respected by every downstream use of the data, including any extract that leaves the warehouse.
The distinction between 'our company only' and 'our company and partners' consent must be carried through to any data sharing decision.
The business must be able to answer, for an individual, what personal data it holds about them across this area, supported by the single view of a party.
requirements.obj: personal data held about an individual

requirements.text: The company-wide party number is assumed to be stable and never re-used for a different party, which must be confirmed with the operational system owners.

business_keys.rationale: REQ-002 states each business entity is identified by a single company-wide number unique across all parties; REQ-003 uses it as the integration point and REQ-065 assumes it is stable and never reused (to be confirmed). Business-recognised, unique, non-null.

REQ-008 states a person is identified by the same company-wide business entity number with no separate person identifier; REQ-009 says every person is a business entity. Stable and unique per REQ-065.
REQ-006 and REQ-007 explicitly state the globally unique record identifier is technical replication metadata, has no business meaning and is not a business key.

REQ-001-2 states each postal address is identified by its own address number; the address is recorded once and shared by multiple parties (REQ-007-2). It is a system-assigned number, but the requirements name it as the identifier and no natural alternative exists.

REQ-015-2 and REQ-011-2 describe a reference list of address types (Billing, Home, Shipping) with descriptive names, and REQ-013-2 uses the type in relationship uniqueness. No explicit code is given, so the ID is the available identifier.
REQ-015-2 gives address types a descriptive name (e.g. Billing, Home, Shipping), which the business recognises. Uniqueness and stability are not stated, and renames can occur.

REQ-035-2 and REQ-036-2 describe a contact type reference list with descriptive names, and REQ-037-2 uses the role in relationship uniqueness. No natural code is given, so the ID is the available identifier.
REQ-036-2 gives each contact type a descriptive name that the business recognises. Uniqueness and stability are not stated.
REQ-039 and REQ-040 describe a phone number type reference list qualifying telephone numbers. No natural code is given, so the ID is the available identifier.
REQ-040 gives each phone number type a name (home, work, mobile). REQ-044 warns that renames affect historical reporting, so the name is not fully stable.
REQ-021-2 states each country or region is identified by its ISO standard code. The code is stable, unique, business-recognised and non-null.
REQ-022-2 states each state or province is identified by its own number. It is the identifier the requirements name, and it is referenced from addresses (REQ-003-2).

REQ-022-2 gives an ISO state or province code. REQ-025-2 and REQ-026-2 say a substituted country code is used where no genuine code exists. That makes it non-unique and unreliable as a sole key. It could be combined with CountryRegionCode.

REQ-032 says a person may have several email addresses, each numbered within the person. REQ-034 says an email address belongs to exactly one person and is meaningless without them. The key is therefore the person number plus the sequence number.

REQ-038, REQ-039 and REQ-042 say a person has several telephone numbers, each qualified by type, and each number belongs to exactly one person. No explicit uniqueness rule is given, so the composite is inferred.

REQ-013-2 explicitly states that the combination of party, address and address type makes a party-address relationship unique. REQ-014-2 requires both relationships to be visible when the same address has two types.
REQ-037-2 explicitly states that the combination of organisation, person and role makes a contact relationship unique. REQ-038-2 allows a person to hold several roles or organisations.

REQ-050 says a credential is attached to a person by the same business entity number and a person has at most one credential. REQ-047, REQ-049 and REQ-061 say the credential content must be excluded from analytical use, so it is probably out of scope.

# ADR-0001: Data Vault model derived from requirements

**Status:** Proposed
**Date:** 2026-10-21
**Decision makers:** Vault-Agent (generated) — pending human review

## Context

This model was derived automatically by the Vault-Agent pipeline from 115 requirement(s) and 18 business key candidate(s). It records the Data Vault 2.0 structures the modeler chose and traces each back to the requirements that justify it.

## Decision

Model the following Data Vault 2.0 structures.

### Hubs (7)

- **hub_business_entity** — business key `BusinessEntityID`. Company-wide party register (customers, vendors, employees, stores, persons). Persons share the same business entity number, so person data attaches here as satellites rather than a separate hub. Email addresses and credentials are keyed by the same number and are declared as feeds so their satellites bind to their own source. Integrated from 4 source(s): BusinessEntity.BusinessEntityID, Person.BusinessEntityID, EmailAddress.BusinessEntityID, Password.BusinessEntityID; canonical staging key column `BUSINESSENTITYID`. _(requirements: REQ-001, REQ-002, REQ-003, REQ-004, REQ-008, REQ-009, REQ-034, REQ-050, REQ-065)_
- **hub_address** — business key `AddressID`. Postal address recorded once and shareable by many parties. _(requirements: REQ-001-2, REQ-007-2)_
- **hub_address_type** — business key `AddressTypeID`. Reference list of address types (Billing, Home, Shipping). _(requirements: REQ-015-2, REQ-011-2, REQ-056)_
- **hub_contact_type** — business key `ContactTypeID`. Reference list of contact roles. _(requirements: REQ-035-2, REQ-036-2, REQ-056)_
- **hub_phone_number_type** — business key `PhoneNumberTypeID`. Reference list of phone number types (home, work, mobile). _(requirements: REQ-039, REQ-040, REQ-056)_
- **hub_country_region** — business key `CountryRegionCode`. Countries and regions identified by ISO code. _(requirements: REQ-021-2, REQ-056)_
- **hub_state_province** — business key `StateProvinceID`. States and provinces identified by their own number. _(requirements: REQ-022-2, REQ-056)_

### Links (5)

- **link_business_entity_address** — connects hub_business_entity, hub_address, hub_address_type. Which addresses a party uses and in what capacity; party+address+type is unique. Unit of work: BusinessEntityID + AddressID + AddressTypeID. _(requirements: REQ-009-2, REQ-010-2, REQ-011-2, REQ-012-2, REQ-013-2, REQ-014-2, REQ-016-2, REQ-017-2, REQ-019-2)_
